1:
What the last days are is settled here against the commoner opinion. Ellicott reports that most commentators refer the phrase to the period immediately before the second coming, and declines it, preferring on the strength of the epistle that calls the writer's own moment the last time to understand a long stretch running from the first advent to the second; he supports it from the rabbinic division of history into this age and the age to come, and from the talmudic scheme of six thousand years, two of chaos, two under the law and two of Messiah. Wesley says flatly that the gospel dispensation beginning at the Lord's death is what is peculiarly so styled, and Henry that gospel times are meant. Calvin makes the phrase cover the universal condition of the Christian church and denies that the writer is comparing his own age with any later one. Clarke alone keeps a second option open, allowing that the words often mean the days of Messiah but are sometimes stretched to the destruction of Jerusalem, that being properly the last days of the Jewish state, and that the phrase may in any case mean a future near or distant. Robertson notes only that the adjective means hard.

Chrysostom will not let the times take the blame. The writer censures not the days nor the seasons but the men of them, since it is our habit to call an age good or evil from what men do in it. He notes that the warning is given three ways, from prophecy, from the past example of those who withstood Moses, and from reasoning about the vessels in a great house, and that repeating it keeps Timothy from being troubled: if such men existed in Moses's day and will exist afterwards, it is no wonder they exist now. Henry makes the same consolation from the parable, that the net was to enclose bad fish with good, so that nobody should think the worse of religion for it; and he insists the danger is not chiefly persecution from outside but corruption within, two traitors inside a garrison doing more harm than an army before it. Calvin gives the prediction a practical edge, that when matters go to our wish we grow careless, so the warning was meant to sharpen diligence and to prepare a pastor for contests rather than to frighten him off. Gill says it was delivered so that they might be fortified against the event.

On the catalogue that follows, Ellicott reports an attempt to sort the vices into three groups of five, six and seven, and rejects it as artificial, since preserving the groups forces a strained sense on some of the terms; he prefers to read the list as the prominent vices then visible on the surface of Christian society. He does trace a chain within it, boasting and pride describing conduct toward other men, blasphemy the same contempt turned upward, and disobedience in children as the natural harvest of a father who will not know God. Selfishness heading the list he calls the true root of all sin, and the love of money its daughter. Barnes enters the necessary qualification: a regard for oneself that secures one's own salvation is proper and injures nobody, and what is condemned is the self-regard that tramples the rights and comforts of others. Robertson notes that the first term occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and that much of the list recurs in the opening chapter of Romans. Clarke supplies etymologies, the proud being airy and trifling persons who are all outside, the unthankful being those without grace or gracefulness, and then declines to aim the passage anywhere: Catholics apply it to Protestants and Protestants to Catholics, and both have been lovers of their own selves. Gill and Wesley agree that the fault is inside the church.
3:
The list is mostly compound adjectives and the commentators work through them by their parts. Clarke takes the first as the absence of the affection parents bear their young and the young their parents, an affection common to every class of animals, so that men lacking it are worse than brutes; Wesley pairs it with the two that follow and gets an antithesis out of them, that such men are both too soft and too hard. The next word Clarke and Robertson both derive from the drink-offering, since libations of blood and wine were poured at the making of treaties, so that the men so named are bound by no promise and held by no engagement; Barnes allows either the implacable, who will not be reconciled, or those who simply disregard agreements, and thinks a society in which no compact holds is at its lowest point. The word for false accusers is the ordinary word for devils, as Barnes and Clarke both note, slander being the devil's proper work. On the last of the group Clarke pauses to admire the language rather than the vice, one Greek word carrying what English needs five or six for, and adds that those who do not love the good must themselves be radically bad. Robertson finds the term nowhere else at all.

Ellicott gives the word for traitors a setting that makes it concrete: it is used of Judas and again of those who betrayed the Just One, and in these years informing against believers and disclosing where they met in time of persecution was profitable work, however despicable. Clarke reaches instead for a national example he plainly cannot forgive, those who delivered up their own king to his enemies, calling it a stain no lapse of ages can wipe out. The next two words are matters of derivation. Heady comes from falling forward, so it means headlong and precipitate, opposed to whatever is deliberate; high-minded comes from smoke, which gives Clarke the frivolously aspiring, full of themselves and empty of all good, and Ellicott the simpler rendering, blinded by pride. On the last pair Clarke admires the Greek again, the two words for lover of pleasure and lover of God standing side by side so that pleasure is plainly the god actually served. Ellicott closes the catalogue by noticing its shape, that it opens with the love of self, which excludes all love of others, and ends with the love of pleasure, which shuts out all love of God.

The last clause is where they part company over whom the passage indicts. Robertson glosses the noun as the outward shape without the reality, and Clarke as a sketch or summary, fitting those who keep all their religion in a creed, a confession, a catechism or a body of divinity while destitute of the life of God, and who go on to deny that such life is to be experienced at all. Barnes and Gill both aim the whole paragraph at one target, Barnes saying there can be little doubt the writer had in view the great apostasy he describes elsewhere and that no body of men has ever been more zealous in keeping up the forms of religion, Gill filling in particulars from the same quarter, children put into cloisters against their will, priests made to quit their wives and call their children spurious, and secrets betrayed that were learnt in confession. Ellicott aims it much nearer home and draws the distinction that makes the passage bite: the similar catalogue in Romans paints the sins of paganism, while this one describes a new paganism going under the name of Christianity. He adds that the response is graded, the pagan to be courteously entreated but these to be openly shunned. Clarke says the same, that the danger is that their outside is fair and they are seldom suspected.
6:
The verb for creeping in is milder in itself than the English suggests, and Barnes says so, listing four renderings from those who have handled it and concluding that the idea of cunning is not certainly in the word though the whole complexion of the passage implies it. Gill notes that the Syriac chose a word connected with the weasel, whose way in is sometimes covered and sometimes open. Ellicott adds the circumstance that gives the phrase force, that women in those countries lived in a seclusion which made real fraud necessary before their apartments could be reached at all. On why women were the target, Barnes observes that the tempter began with Eve rather than Adam and that the advocates of error have followed the precedent, working through the weaker to reach the men. Ellicott is more specific about the method, that these teachers won their following by supplying anodynes for consciences already burdened. Robertson calls the diminutive contemptuous, records the suggestion that it means something like society ladies, and does not confine the problem to antiquity, naming two religious impostors of his own country and century who gathered women about them under the guise of religion.

The description of perpetual learning without arrival draws the same complaint from several of them. Robertson calls it a pathetic picture of women who lack the intellectual power to cut through a fog of words, always acquiring scraps and never the full knowledge, and adds that they take themselves for the intelligent party. Ellicott finds the motive in a morbid love of novelty and a hope of penetrating mysteries not revealed to true teachers, and holds that the failure was moral, the heart being hardened by the life. Gill divides the blame between the teachers heaped up, who are blind guides, and the hearers, whose own lusts keep them from arriving. Clarke turns it on the ordinary congregation instead: there are many who hear good sermons repeatedly and derive little profit, having no more grace now than years ago, because they do not meditate, do not think, and do not reduce what they hear to practice; under the preaching of an apostle they would still not become wise to salvation. Barnes makes the same extension, that many learn the doctrines speculatively, or the government of the church, or the philosophical theories of religion, and remain strangers to the thing itself. Wesley compresses it to learning new things but not the truth of God.

The two names are not in the Old Testament and everyone says so. Barnes holds the tradition sound anyway, since nothing is likelier than that the names of the chief magicians who tried to match the miracles would be kept, and points to Jewish sources and to three pagan or early Christian writers who mention them. Ellicott traces the names to the Targum and reports the legends that made the men sons of Balaam and first the instructors and afterwards the enemies of Moses, one story drowning them in the Red Sea; he adds that the comparison would strike a boy raised on those histories with particular force, and guesses it was repeated in Christian assemblies long after. Robertson notes that the same verb for withstanding is used of the sorcerer struck blind in Acts, and Ellicott that the claim to occult arts is what makes the comparison apt. On the promise that they shall proceed no further, Ellicott takes it as comfort deliberately offered after an unsparing diagnosis, and observes that the prophecy has held, one school of error after another passing into disrepute and then oblivion while the church remains. Barnes states it as a general law that error is plausible at first and always at length seen to be folly. Gill measures the limit by the precedent, that the magicians hardened Pharaoh but could not keep Israel from departing.
10:
The verb behind "fully known" means to follow alongside, and Ellicott and Barnes both make the point that the sense is tracing something out step by step rather than merely being informed of it; Ellicott cites the preface of the third gospel, where the same word describes an author who has traced events back to their source. Robertson counts nine nouns governed by it, seven belonging to this verse and two to the next. Ellicott finds two purposes in the appeal: to set the writer's life against the lives of the men just described, and to make the old man's endurance a spur to the disciple. Clarke expands the list into a usable contrast, since Timothy had seen the doctrine, the conduct founded on it, the object in view, the fidelity, the long-suffering toward opponents and the patience in adversity, and could judge between his teacher and the false ones. Henry draws a rule out of it, that the more fully the doctrine is known the more closely men cleave to it, and that those who sit loose to it do so because they do not know it fully. Gill explains why it is called "my doctrine" at all, not as invented but as received and preached without adulteration.

The three cities are named rather than any others, and Ellicott asks why. His answer has two parts: for a general reader the events there were fair samples of what had happened often since, but for this reader they were the first cities of the first missionary journey, and some of the incidents were among his earliest memories of the work while others happened just before he was taken as a companion. Barnes and Gill supply what happened, the Jews stirring up the leading men at Antioch in Pisidia, the assault at Iconium, and the stoning at Lystra where the writer was dragged out for dead; and both note that this was Timothy's own country, so he had the story from witnesses if not from sight. Clarke goes through the same three from the narrative in Acts and adds that the party afterwards returned to all three cities where they had so lately been persecuted. Robertson notes that the verb for the deliverance which follows is used again at the end of this letter of the Lord's rescuing, and that the phrase in the earlier letter about what befell him gives a fuller account.

The general rule that follows is stated by all of them without softening. Ellicott insists the writer would not have it thought that his own case was singular, and takes the added phrase about being in Christ to mean there is no true piety outside communion with him. Robertson glosses the participle as those who determine to live godly and renders the verb as being hunted like wild beasts. Wesley makes it an instruction to count the cost and leaves no room for exceptions: either scripture fails, or those who think themselves religious and are not persecuted in some shape deceive themselves. Clarke gives the reason in a sentence, that if religion gives no quarter to vice, the vicious will give none to religion. Barnes defines what persecution is with some care, that it consists in subjecting a man to injury or disadvantage on account of his opinions, which is a different thing from meeting those opinions with argument. On the men growing worse, Barnes states it as the law of an unconverted nature, that progress downward is certain though gradual, and adds that Timothy was not to expect relief from any improvement in them. Robertson derives the word for seducers from professional mourners and so from deceivers and jugglers, and Clarke from pretenders to magic. Wesley finds the saddest point in the last clause, that a man who has begun to deceive others is the less likely to recover from his own error.
14:
The pronoun sets the contrast: the others go from bad to worse, but thou abide. Robertson marks the emphatic construction and notes that the verb for being assured is a rare one meaning to be made reliable. Ellicott draws from the imperative a principle about the content rather than the man, that however the opposition intensifies there is to be no development in the fundamental doctrines. Clarke keeps the warning personal instead, that no man however well instructed or grounded is beyond the reach of temptation and final ruin, so that watching and persevering remain necessary. Gill treats the whole verse as an exhortation suitable to every age and reads what follows as the reasons enforcing it. Of whom the teaching was learned is a textual question. Ellicott reports the older authorities nearly balanced between singular and plural, adopts the singular with the Latin and Syriac versions and refers it to the apostle, and adds that if the plural stood the reference would probably be to him and a fellow-missionary. Wesley takes the singular the same way and glosses it as from a teacher approved of God.

Ellicott then rejects outright the reading others build on, that the mother and grandmother are meant. He thinks such a reminiscence, however touching, too slight to be introduced into so solemn an exhortation, and holds that family memories are covered by the verse immediately following. Barnes takes precisely the position rejected, referring the clause to the mother as well as the apostle, and draws a doctrine from it: that having received the truth from a parent's lips is a strong reason for holding to it, since a parent has no motive to deceive a child and has usually had far better opportunity of examining what is true. He is careful to add that this is not the highest motive and does not bind a man to what he later finds erroneous. Robertson widens the list further still, to the prophets, the apostle, and both the women by name, and remarks that there ought to be moral authority in such personages. On the early teaching itself the sources agree and quote the same rabbinic tradition: Barnes gives the maxim that a boy of five should study the scriptures, and the harder saying that a father who does not teach his son the law when the child begins to talk seems rather to bury him; Gill cites the Alexandrian for instruction from very infancy.

The phrase for the writings is unusual. Ellicott and Robertson both note that it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though it is used by Josephus, and Robertson adds a local contrast that gives the term an edge: at Ephesus there were famous writings too, but those were profane where these are sacred. All agree that what is meant is the Old Testament, since nothing else was extant in Timothy's infancy, which Wesley states and then turns into an argument from the lesser to the greater, that if those alone could make a child wise unto salvation, how much more can both Testaments together. Barnes examines the word for child and finds it used of the unborn, of infants and of sucklings, so that an early age is denoted without a precise one. Robertson dates the teaching from the fifth year and breaks off to wish that parents took like pains now. Clarke is firm that no soul is made wise unto salvation by those scriptures except as it refers everything to Christ, which is why the Jews who know them well remain unsaved; Robertson says the same more briefly, that their use was not magic but of value through faith. Henry gives the practical form: the age of children is the age to learn, the books must not lie neglected, and the greatest kindness we can do children is to make them early know the Bible.
16:
The famous sentence turns on where the verb "is" belongs, since the Greek supplies none. Robertson sets the problem out without taking a side: the article is absent, and there are examples of that construction going both ways, so the words may be rendered either all scripture or every scripture, and the copula may be inserted before the conjunction or after it, giving either a flat assertion that all scripture is inspired and profitable, or a statement that every inspired scripture is also profitable. Ellicott chooses the second and argues for it twice over, from the Syriac and Latin versions and a line of expositors, and then on a ground of sense that is his own: a declaration of the inspiration of the Jewish scriptures would have been uncalled for here, since a trained Jew of that century would never have dreamt of doubting it and nothing in the preceding verses provokes the assertion. Clarke agrees on the rendering, observing that the conjunction is dropped by almost all the versions and many of the fathers and does not sit well in the text. Barnes takes the received reading and treats the verse as the apostle's solemn testimony that the whole of the older canon is inspired.

How far the word reaches is a second quarrel. Barnes and Clarke both restrict it to the Old Testament, Clarke because the New was neither collected nor complete, Barnes adding that if the writer was himself inspired the verse settles the question for the older canon. Ellicott restricts the subject the same way while noting that his preferred rendering does not exclude the recent compositions whose divine origin the writer knew, having seen or written them. Gill goes the other way outright, taking the words of the whole of holy scripture, New as well as Old, most of which he thinks was written by then, and extending the principle to what remained to be written. On the compound adjective Barnes traces it to God and the verb to breathe, recalls the breath into the nostrils of Adam and the breathing on the disciples, and finds parallels in a Greek moralist and in the Roman who spoke of a poet filled as by some divine spirit; but he stops short of method, insisting the word asserts a fact and tells us nothing of how inspiration worked. Clarke names the two accounts men have given, dictation of every thought and word, or the matter given and the language left to the writer, which he thinks explains the variety of style.

Wesley adds a claim the others do not make, that the Spirit who once inspired the writers continually assists those who read with earnest prayer. Gill commends the writings from internal marks, a majesty of style inimitable in many places and a sublimity of matter no human capacity could have discovered. Chrysostom supplies the reason for reaching to the scriptures here, that the writer has a hard thing to say next about his own death and softens it first; he measures the disciple's grief by the prophet who rent his garments when his master was taken from him. Who the man of God is then divides them. Gill takes it of anyone in special relation to God but chiefly of a minister, the title having passed over from the prophets; Clarke restricts it to the preacher who derives his commission from God; Ellicott denies that it is an official designation at all and makes it the Christian generally. On the two closing adjectives Clarke gives the arithmetic sense of a whole number to which nothing need be added, and Robertson that the first is from a root meaning to fit and the second a rare verb for furnishing out completely. Barnes ends where the argument points, that no situation in life finds the book deficient and no progress in knowledge or holiness outruns it.
